paper_title: Understanding Multimodality in Generative Behavioral Cloning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Behavioral cloning becomes challenging when the same observation admits several valid actions. We study how generative behavioral-cloning policies represent such multimodal expert behavior and identify different bottlenecks across model parameterizations. For latent-variable policies, preserving demonstrated modes requires action-conditioned information in the latent representation. Excessive posterior-prior regularization can suppress this information and prevent the policy from distinguishing demonstrated modes. Weaker or aggregate regularization can preserve mode information, but shifts the challenge to ensuring that the deployment-time prior covers the relevant latent regions. For action-space generative policies, multimodality is constrained by the smoothness of the base-to-action transport: a map with a small Lipschitz constant cannot assign substantial probability to many well-separated modes. Covering many modes therefore requires either sharp transitions in base space or off-support bridge regions in action space. Experiments on synthetic multimodal navigation and a physical-robot bimodal manipulation task support these mechanisms. In contrast, our analysis reveals limited conditional multimodality in standard robotic simulation benchmarks, where deterministic regression remains competitive.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Imitation learning trains robot policy directly from expert demonstrations [24, 28, 12]. standard approach is behavioral cloning (BC), which fits policy to observationaction pairs collected under an expert policy, without the need for online interaction, reward engineering, or exploration. Due to its practical appeal, BC has become dominant paradigm for training deep visuomotor policies in robotic manipulation [43, 7, 37, 16, 2]. Recent work on behavioral cloning has highlighted multimodality in the experts conditional action distribution as central challenge [10, 31, 7, 19, 32]: for the same observation, the dataset may contain multiple valid actions. This may arise from different expert styles, equally good choices, or latent factors absent from the observation space [20]. Under an L2 or unimodal-Gaussian behavioral-cloning head, the maximum-likelihood solution regresses to the conditional mean of the modes, which is typically not an element of any modes support [41, 10]. canonical example is inverse kinematics in robot control[1]: the same end-effector target may admit disconnected joint-space solutions. Averaging can yield joint command that lies on none of the inverse-kinematics branches, while filtering to one branch removes feasible alternatives needed under constraints such as obstacles or joint limits. Corresponding authors. 1NCT/UCC Dresden, UKDD Dresden, TU Dresden, DKFZ Heidelberg. 2Ludwig-MaximiliansUniversität München, Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML). 3BMFTR Research Hub 6G-Life. 4Cluster of Excellence CeTI. 5University of Tromsø. 6German Aerospace Center (DLR). 7HZDR Dresden. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Contemporary multimodal BC methods typically predict short chunks of future actions rather than single-step actions, improving temporal coherence while enabling one-shot non-autoregressive inference over the chunk [43, 7]. There are two broad approaches to making such policies multimodal: latent-variable methods and action-space generative methods. Latent-variable methods introduce an unobserved code, continuous or discrete, from which different action chunks can be decoded [43, 19, 40]. Action-space generative methods model the distribution over action chunks directly, using flows or diffusion models [7, 2, 23]. Both approaches can generate diverse actions, and their multimodality is typically evaluated by rollout performance. In both approaches, however, it remains unclear which modeland training-level quantities control the multimodality of the learned policy. Our goal is to fill this gap by providing precise definition of multimodality. Furthermore, we identify the key quantities that must be controlled to preserve multimodality: the posteriorprior regularization strength in CVAE-based policies, and the Lipschitz constant of the base-to-action map in action-space generators. Contribution. We study how posterior-prior regularization affects multimodality in action-chunking behavioral cloning. For latent-variable policies, we show that preserving demonstrated modes requires action-conditioned latent information; see Proposition 1. We then show that pointwise posteriorprior regularization can suppress this information as its strength increases, giving the multimodality collapse criterion in Corollary 2. For action-space generators, we show that deterministic sampler with small Lipschitz constant is more likely to assign small probability to many modes; see Proposition 2, losing multimodality. Therefore, regularization methods that enforce small Lipschitz constant tend to suppress multimodality. We empirically validate these mechanisms on controlled multimodal navigation and manipulation tasks and provide practical heuristics. We also introduce diagnostic for conditional multimodality in robot demonstration datasets. Applied to standard robotic simulation benchmarks, it detects limited conditional multimodality, while our policy evaluations show that deterministic regression remains competitive. We release the code used in the experiments1. Structure of the paper. Section 2 defines multimodal behavioral cloning over actions and the generative policy families considered in the paper. Section 3 formalizes mode preservation and proves that latent policies must carry action-conditioned mode information, leading to collapse criterion for pointwise prior regularization, latent-geometry condition for aggregate matching, and Lipschitz lower bound for action-space generators. Section 4 introduces controlled synthetic benchmarks with ground-truth mode labels and evaluates representative methods on synthetic and robotic tasks to test whether these mechanisms explain practical failures. Notation, proofs, related works, and experimental details are described in the Appendices.

sections.content: Synthetic navigation tasks. We design four 2D multimodal navigation tasks with ground-truth modes (Figure 1), which allow us to test five research questions from the theory: (RQ1) Is mode coverage necessary for successful rollouts when the true data distribution is multimodal? (RQ2) Do the lower bounds from Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 hold in practice, and how tight are they? (RQ3) How can we provide practical recipes to pick value for the KL regularizer β? (RQ4, Appendix E.4) Can aggregate posterior matching preserve latent mode information, and how does the geometry of the deployment prior interact with the training posterior? (RQ5) What are the practical consequences of the relationship between Lθ,s and the number of τ -represented modes (τ ) of the action-space generators identified by Proposition 2? θ Simulated and real-world robot demonstrations. While the synthetic tasks provide groundtruth modes for testing the theory, robot demonstration datasets typically lack such labels. We therefore introduce heuristic to estimate the conditional action multimodality of demonstration dataset. This enables us to study the interaction between the multimodality of the policies and the eventual multimodality of the training demonstrations. In simulation, we use Push-T [7], UR3 BlockPush [10], LIBERO[21], Meta-World [42], and Kitchen [11], benchmarks previously used to evaluate multimodal and vision-language policies [7, 19, 30, 32]. Surprisingly, despite their use in prior work to evaluate policies designed to capture multimodality [7, 31, 19, 32], most simulation benchmarks have almost-unimodal support across the dataset states. In our proof-of-concept robot dataset of bimodal tissue grasping, the multimodality is higher, and when the action horizon is long enough, it approximates the ground-truth value of 2 semantic modes. Policy performance. We evaluate the baseline policies on the simulation and robot benchmarks (Fig. 4 and Appendix E.7). We emphasize here that our goal is not to obtain state-of-the-art performance, but to study how (estimated) multimodality of each robot benchmarks data distribution interacts with different policy parametrizations, and whether policy parametrizations that can represent this property lead to better downstream performance. The largest performance gap between regression and multimodal-capable policies occurs on bimodal tissue grasping, the dataset with the highest estimated multimodality: BCAT averages the two modes and achieves 0% success. parametrization unable to represent conditional multimodality cannot recover the full conditional expert distribution when the latter exhibits distinct modes. Mode averaging may still yield successful rollouts if the interpolation happens to be valid, but this reflects fortuitous compatibility with the task constraints rather than faithful, safe imitation. Mode coverage, however, is not necessary condition for success: Sinkhorn-CWAE collapses to single mode during training and still retains 85% success. On the other hand, on the estimated nearly unimodal simulation data, deterministic regression remains competitive, while multimodal-capable policies can improve or worsen performance, depending on their training dynamics, and generally increase inference latency. This is consistent with concurrent work [22], which attributes benefits of flow-based policies on common BC benchmarks primarily to supervised iterative computation and training-time noise injection rather than the representation of multimodal action distributions supposedly present in the data.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we formalize multimodality in imitation learning and show that, for both CVAE-based and action-space generative policies, mode preservation is governed by explicit quantities. For CVAEs, the key factor is posterior-prior regularization: stronger regularization improves alignment but can remove the action-conditioned information needed to recover distinct modes. For actionspace generative policies with deterministic samplers, the key factor is the Lipschitz constant of the base-to-action map: excessive smoothness prevents assigning significant mass to many well-separated modes. To further emphasize the practical relevance of our analysis, we note that the default choice of β is 10 in ACT [43]. Our analysis reveals that this choice is likely to produce unimodal policies. We empirically validate this in Section 4.1. On the simulation benchmarks, our diagnostics detect little conditional multimodality, and deterministic regression remains competitive. These findings suggest that representing multiple action modes may not be the main bottleneck for policy performance in these settings. 9 Figure 4: Policy success rate on robot benchmarks, normalized to [0, 1]. Limitations and future work. Current limitations are that our results are training-independent: Corollary 2 does not ensure that training finds an optimizer (ˆθ, ˆϕ, ˆψ) with the desired multimodal properties, while Proposition 2 only identifies structural limitation of low-Lipschitz samplers. Since common regularizers penalize Lipschitz behavior, they may bias policies toward mode collapse. Future work will examine how to estimate the number of modes for datasets where only visual features are available, develop training procedures that balance sampler smoothness and mode preservation, and understand whether the limited conditional multimodality observed in robotic simulation benchmarks also characterizes large-scale real-robot datasets.

sections.title: C Related work
sections.content: Multimodal BC has been modeled through several policy families. ACT uses KL-regularized CVAE with an explicit latent variable to represent trajectory style [43]. VQ-BeT represents multimodality through learned discrete latent tokens and two-stage training recipe [19, 30]. Q-FAT uses continuous Gaussian-mixture heads in an autoregressive transformer [32], which is structurally slower than parallel action-chunk decoding. Implicit BC parameterizes the policy as conditional energy function, requiring sampling or gradient-based optimization at inference rather than single decoder pass [10]. More recent methods shift multimodality directly into action-space denoising or flow matching [7, 26, 25, 2, 23, 33]. Across these approaches, comparisons remain largely task-driven and empirical, with limited theoretical guidance on which training quantities affect policies ability to represent multimodality. For one-shot push-forward generators = Gθ(s, ), existing results show that separated multimodal targets force trade-off between approximation error and generator smoothness [29]. For iterative samplers such as DDIM [7] or deterministic flow solvers [2, 23, 33], we study this trade-off for the composed deterministic sampling map induced by the denoising or flow updates. parallel gap appears in latent-based policies: pointwise KL regularization is standard, but its weight is usually treated as an empirical hyperparameter.

D.2 Network Architectures This section describes the neural implementations, the benchmarks, and the training and evaluation details of the experiments. All policies predict action chunks non-autoregressively. Within each benchmark, methods share the same observation encoder, action representation, normalization pipeline, and training loop, and differ only in the output parameterization. 29 Observation encoders. Image observations are encoded with convolutional encoder, initialized from pretrained weights and fine-tuned during policy training. The encoder preserves the spatial feature map, uses no global pooling, and uses frozen batch-normalization statistics. Proprioceptive and state observations are encoded with single projection layer. Action decoder. The deterministic and latent-variable policies use non-autoregressive action transformer decoders. Encoded observations are first converted into token sequence. Spatial feature maps receive two-dimensional sinusoidal positional encodings, while flat features receive one-dimensional positional encodings. Let RHd denote the learnable action-query sequence, with one query embedding per predicted action timestep. Given the observation-token sequence, the decoder maps to action embeddings in parallel, and task-specific action heads map these embeddings to the predicted action components. The deterministic baseline uses the non-latent version of this decoder. For an observation s, the action transformer produces action embeddings U1:H = Dθ(Q, Xs), where Xs RNsd denotes the encoded observation tokens. The action heads then produce single predicted chunk, ˆa = Headθ(U1:H) = fθ(s). LACT. Latent-variable policies use LACT, latent-conditioned variant of the previous action decoder. Given latent z, LACT conditions each decoder block through AdaLN-Zero-style modulation, as used in DiT-style transformers. The conditioning network maps to scale, shift, and residualgating parameters, which modulate the normalization and residual branches of the self-attention, cross-attention, and feedforward blocks. Thus, the latent affects the full action-query decoding process, and the decoder implements the map ˆa = fθ(z, s). MMDiT action decoder. Action-space flow and diffusion policies use an MMDiT-style dual-stream transformer [8]. The model receives observation tokens and action tokens as separate streams. The action stream contains either interpolated actions for flow matching or noisy actions for diffusion. timestep embedding conditions the transformer layers through adaptive normalization. The dualstream decoder allows bidirectional attention between observation and action tokens, and final prediction layer maps the action-token outputs to either velocities for Act-Flow or denoising targets for Act-Diff. For Act-Flow, the MMDiT predicts the action-space velocity field used by the flow solver. For Act-Diff, the MMDiT predicts the diffusion training target and is sampled with deterministic DDIM scheduler. Latent encoders. Latent-variable policies use transformer encoders to parameterize the posterior and, when used, the learned prior. The posterior encoder receives sequence of tokens containing the ground-truth action sequence together with the encoded observation tokens. learnable class token is appended to the sequence, and transformer encoder maps the final class-token representation to the latent output. For KL-CVAE, the posterior projection has output dimension 2dz and is split into mean and log-variance, (µϕ(a, s), ℓϕ(a, s)) = Pϕ(CLSϕ(a, s)) , which define the diagonal Gaussian posterior qϕ( a, s). For aggregate-matched variants and LAT-Flow, the projection has output dimension dz and directly returns zq = eϕ(a, s). The VQ-VAE posterior uses the same action-plus-observation transformer encoder, but replaces the continuous latent output by residual vector-quantized bottleneck. The class-token representation is first projected to continuous vector zcont = Pϕ(CLSϕ(a, s)), 30 which is then quantized by residual codebook stack. The quantized latent zq is passed to the action decoder. Learned priors use separate transformer encoder that receives only observation tokens. class token is appended to the observation sequence, and the final class-token representation is projected to prior parameters, (µψ(s), ℓψ(s)) = Pψ(CLSψ(s)) , defining pψ( s) = (µψ(s), diag exp ℓψ(s)) . For conditional aggregate matching, the same prior encoder also emits an action-free condition vector hη(s). This vector is obtained by pooling the observation tokens and used to compute the conditional MMD/Sinkhorn losses. D.3 Benchmarks All benchmarks use observation horizon Tobs = 1. Thus, each policy conditions on single current observation, without observation history. The action horizon depends on the benchmark. Synthetic tasks use = 60, corresponding to the full task trajectory. Simulation and real-world robot benchmarks use = 10; at evaluation time, we execute the first two actions from each predicted chunk before replanning. Synthetic benchmark. The synthetic benchmark consists of four 2D navigation tasks. All trajectories lie in the unit square [0, 1]2. Each task contains 1000 demonstrations. Policies receive single 64 64 RGB rendering at = 0, showing the agent initial position, obstacles, and goal regions, and predict the complete trajectory chunk a0:H1 R602, with = 60, without replanning. Thus, each trajectory effectively contains one single training sample pair. The four tasks differ in their mode structure. Circle has = 2 circular trajectory modes around obstacles. Sequential has two consecutive binary decisions, yielding = 4 modes separated by three obstacles. Radial has = 16 modes from common start to sixteen evenly spaced radial goals, with obstacles between neighboring directions. Corridor has = 16 valid routes from common start to common endpoint through sixteen corridors induced by fifteen obstacles. For synthetic evaluation, generated trajectory is successful if it satisfies all three criteria: it does not collide with obstacles; its endpoint is within distance 0.1 of one valid mode endpoint; and its path length is at least 0.8 times the mean expert path length. The path-length condition rules out trivial collapsed trajectories that reach an endpoint without following valid path. We also report valid mode coverage and valid mode entropy ratio, computed only over successful trajectories. Simulation benchmarks. We use PushT, Franka Kitchen, and UR3 BlockPush as robotic simulation benchmarks previously employed in the literature of multimodal policy [10, 7, 30, 19, 32], together with the language-conditioned benchmarks LIBERO and Meta-World, extensively used in the visionlanguage-action model benchmarking, see for example [2, 33]. PushT requires pushing T-shaped block to target pose using 2D end-effector control [7]. We use both image and state variants. The image observation is single 96 96 RGB agent-view image. The state observation contains the end-effector position, block position, block angle, block keypoints, and contact indicator. PushT performance is measured by final intersection-over-union (IoU) between the block pose and target pose. Franka Kitchen [11] is long-horizon manipulation environment in which Franka arm completes subset of kitchen subtasks in sequence. We use state and image variants. The state observation contains 9 robot-arm configuration variables and 21 object configuration variables. The image observation is single 112 112 RGB rendering. Performance is reported as the number of completed goals out of four. UR3 BlockPush requires moving two blocks to two target regions. The task is multimodal because the blocks can be pushed in different orders. We use the unconditional state variant. The state contains the 2D end-effector position and the 2D positions of both blocks; the action is 2D end-effector target. Performance is reported as the number of achieved goals out of two. LIBERO [21] is language-specified robotic manipulation benchmark. We train one policy on four suites with ten tasks each: LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Long. The first three suites vary spatial relationships, manipulated objects, and task goals, respectively, while LIBERO-Long emphasizes longer-horizon manipulation. Meta-World [42] comprises 50 robotic manipulation tasks performed by simulated Sawyer arm. Its four-dimensional action space consists of three-dimensional end-effector displacements and gripper command. We train on the MT50 Figure 5: Real-world surgical robot task: bimodal tissue grasping. Real-world benchmark: bimodal tissue grasping To validate the policies on real-world robotic platform, we design the surgical task of bimodal tissue grasping. During minimally invasive surgery for gastrointestinal cancer, surgical assistants commonly manipulate and retract the small bowel to expose the surgical field for procedures such as anastomosis and tumor resection [17]. In the bimodal bowel tissue grasping task, segment of bowel tissue must be grasped and displaced while avoiding sensitive region of interest, representing, for example, tumor or another area where grasping could cause tissue trauma. Two separate safe grasping regions are available and located on opposite sides of the region of interest. Both grasps are equally valid, but they correspond to distinct trajectory strategies, for example, reflecting left-side versus right-side approach preferences. The resulting conditional action-chunk distribution is therefore bimodal. We collect 90 demonstrations, balanced across the two modes with 45 demonstrations per mode, using an open-source surgical robotics platform [27] and the Open-HELP abdominal phantom [15]. picture of the setup can be seen in Figure 5. The observation space comprises the current Cartesian 3D position of the surgical instrument tip and the binary gripper state; the action space is the delta 3D movement of the tip and the binary gripper action. 32 D.4 Training Details All runs used 32-bit precision. All policies in given benchmark share the same observation representation, normalization, action horizon, data loader, optimizer, and training loop. The network architectures are described in Appendix D.2. The full hyperparameter tables are reported in Appendix F. Each experiment was executed as single-GPU job on an NVIDIA H100 94GB GPU. The available memory was not fully utilized for smaller models; in particular, synthetic runs required less than 4GB of VRAM. Synthetic experiments used 8 CPU workers per job and required approximately 2040 minutes of wall-clock time. Simulation and robot experiments used 14 CPU workers per job and required approximately 1020 hours of wall-clock time, depending on the benchmark and model family. D.5 Evaluation Details Policies are evaluated by rolling them out in the benchmark environments on which they were trained. For the synthetic benchmarks, we perform 200 rollouts per policy every 100 epochs and report each metric as the average over the last five evaluation checkpoints, corresponding to 5 200 = 1000 rollouts. For the simulation benchmarks, we evaluate each policy on 200 rollout trials using reproducible random seed that is varied per each roll-out, in order to sample reproducibly randomized initial conditions. We repeat the evaluation over three seeds. We evaluate policies at fixed and latest checkpoint intervals. For the real-robot experiment, we evaluate each policy for 20 trials.

BCAT performs reasonably well across the simulation benchmarks, consistent with limited conditional action multimodality in their demonstration data. It also achieves higher average inference throughput than the flow-matching and CVAE policies evaluated here. The choice of multimodal-capable policy should therefore be informed by whether the demonstration data actually require this representational capacity. 2. The performance of multimodal-capable policies varies with training dynamics. Latentvariable policies involve many hyperparameters, resulting in large search space for an effective configuration. Action-space flow or diffusion policies may therefore be preferable when reducing this tuning burden is priority. 3. Some models collapse late in training, including Act-Flow on UR3 BlockPush and KLCVAE-LP on Kitchen Image. These observations highlight the importance of checkpoint selection and motivate further investigation of the role of covariate shift [28, 18] in performance degradation. 4. As emphasized in the manuscript, the bimodal tissue-grasping task illustrates the consequences of failing to represent certified multimodal demonstrations. BCAT collapses toward an average between modes, whereas Sinkhorn-CWAE-LP collapses to single demonstrated mode. In this case, single-mode collapse retains demonstrated strategy rather than interpolating into region outside the expert support. Although Sinkhorn-CWAE-LP does not recover the full multimodal behavior, it still achieves an 85% success rate. E.8 Relationship between policy performance and action horizon This ablation examines how policy performance varies with the training and execution action horizons. As noted in the manuscript, the multimodality of the demonstration data is horizon-dependent. We investigate how the choice of training horizon affects policy performance and how this interacts with the execution horizon, which determines the frequency of replanning. The results in Table 16 show that longer open-loop execution amplifies failure but does not fully explain it. Performance generally deteriorates at longer execution horizons, particularly for long training chunks, consistent with the accumulation of open-loop errors. However, longer training chunks can also reduce performance at fixed, short execution horizon, suggesting that modeling longer, higher-dimensional, and potentially more multimodal action distributions introduces additional difficulty. Training horizons of around 10 actions and execution horizons of 25 actions typically yield the best performance. This suggests double trade-off: during training, short chunks provide limited temporal consistency but are easier to model, while long chunks teach policies temporal coherence of the actions but need to learn higher-dimensional conditional distribution. During execution, short horizons enable frequent replanning, improving reactivity and limiting the accumulation of deployment errors, but reduce sustained commitment to global strategy. Longer execution horizons instead enforce commitment to longer-term plan, at the cost of accumulating open-loop errors. sections.content: We report the hyperparameters used across synthetic and simulation experiments. dash denotes setting that is not applicable or not run. Unless stated otherwise, all models use AdamW with learning rate 5 104, weight decay 0.02, observation horizon Tobs = 1, and action horizon = 10 for simulation and robot tasks. Synthetic tasks use = 60. Image encoders are fine-tuned jointly with the policy. All transformer layers use ReLU as activation function. Latent and generative objectives. For KL-CVAE, the pointwise KL weight is βKL = 0.01. Learned-prior KL variants use conditional Gaussian prior with fixed unit variance. For VQ-VAE, the commitment weight is βvq = 0.25 and the number of residual quantization layers is Lvq = 2. For aggregate-matched latent models, posterior geometry regularization uses decoder-side latent jitter σdec = 0.075, mean penalty weight βmean = 0.01, standard-deviation penalty weight βstd = 0.05, covariance penalty weight βcov = 0.01, target standard deviation σ = 1, and maximum standard deviation σmax = 2. Learned latent priors are matched to posterior means. For MMD-CWAE and its conditional variant, the latent aggregate matching weight is β = 1.0. We use the inverse multiquadratic kernel [38] kIMQ(z, z) = (cid:88) CCz + z2 2 . For synthetic experiments, Cz = {0.5dz, dz, 2dz, 4dz}. For simulation and robot experiments, Cz = {dz, 2dz, 4dz, 8dz}. For Sinkhorn-CWAE and its conditional variant, the latent aggregate matching weight is β = 0.01, the blur parameter is εSink = 0.1, and the transport cost is squared Euclidean distance. For both conditional aggregate matching models (Appendix D.1) used in the simulation experiments, the state-conditioning weight is λs = 1.0. For LAT-Flow, the latent flow-prior loss weight is βflow = 0.01. LAT-Flow and Act-Flow both use an Euler solver with 10 inference steps and sample training times from Beta(1.5, 1). For Act-Diff, we use DDIM scheduler with 100 training timesteps and 100 inference steps, the squared-cosine capped noise schedule, sample prediction, sample clipping enabled, α0 = 1, and step offset 0. Dropout. Synthetic action decoders use dropout 0.2 and attention dropout 0.05. Simulation and robot action decoders use dropout 0.1 and attention dropout 0.01. Posterior encoders use dropout 0.2 and attention dropout 0.05. Learned-prior encoders use dropout 0.1 and attention dropout 0.01. Data augmentation and normalization. sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and Section 1 state the papers scope: an analysis of multimodality in behavioral cloning across latent-variable and action-space generative action-chunking policies. The theoretical claims are formalized in Section 3 and Appendix B, and the empirical claims are evaluated in Section 4 and additionally in Appendix E. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The conclusion highlights the main limitations: the strongest mode-level diagnostics rely on controlled synthetic tasks with known mode labels and simulation benchmarks. It also identifies extensions to richer real-world mode annotations and broader policy classes as future work. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover 48 limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 3 states the assumptions and results for the latent-information bounds, aggregate matching, and action-space geometric cost. Full proofs and supporting notation and definitions are provided in Appendix and B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4 describes the benchmark structure, evaluated policy families, and main metrics. Appendices D, and provide additional architecture, training, diagnostic, and evaluation details. Exact bitwise reproducibility is not guaranteed because some GPU operations may be nondeterministic, but the reported protocols and aggregate metrics are reproducible in expectation. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. 49 While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide as supplementary material downloadable ZIP archive for the code, synthetic data-generation scripts, simulation datasets, simulation benchmark evaluation servers, diagnostic scripts, README and reproduction instructions. The archive is anonymized and contains no author-identifying metadata. Upon acceptance, we will release the final public version. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] 50 Justification: The experimental setup is summarized in Section 4.
